How to Prevent Bed Bugs From Entering Your Home

Bed bug prevention isn't about sprays or old wives' tales — it's about understanding how these pests actually travel and stopping them before they establish a foothold in your home. Once bed bugs settle in, treatment costs can easily exceed $1,000 for a moderate infestation. The good news? Most infestations are preventable if you know what to look for and take a few simple precautions.

Shaw's Pest Control has been protecting Wichita-area homes since 1987, and our Master Tech–certified technicians have seen how a single overlooked suitcase or secondhand dresser can turn into a month-long ordeal. This guide covers the real-world prevention strategies that keep bed bugs out — from travel habits to furniture inspection to early detection tactics that catch problems before they become expensive.

How Bed Bugs Actually Spread (And Why It Matters)

Bed bugs don't fly, jump, or live on your body. They're hitchhikers. They spread by crawling into luggage, purses, backpacks, clothing, or furniture — then riding along until they find a new place to hide and feed. Understanding this behavior is the foundation of effective bed bug prevention.

The three most common entry points are travel accommodations, secondhand furniture, and visitors. Hotels and short-term rentals are prime transfer zones because bed bugs move between rooms via luggage and personal belongings. A single female bed bug can lay 200–500 eggs in her lifetime, so even one hitchhiker can become an infestation within weeks.

Secondhand furniture — especially upholstered pieces, bed frames, and dressers — is another major vector. Bed bugs hide in seams, joints, and cracks, making them nearly invisible during a casual inspection. Even high-end furniture can harbor bed bugs if it came from an infested home.

Finally, guests can unknowingly bring bed bugs into your home. If someone visiting you has an active infestation at their residence, bed bugs can transfer via their bag, coat, or even the seams of their pants. This doesn't mean you should ban visitors — just be aware that infestations can spread through social contact, especially if someone is living in an infested apartment building.

Hotel and Travel Inspection Checklist

Every time you check into a hotel, Airbnb, or guest room, spend three minutes inspecting before you unpack. Leave your luggage in the bathroom or on a hard, smooth surface (like a desk or luggage rack) while you check the sleeping area.

Pull back the sheets and inspect the mattress seams, particularly at the corners. Look for small rust-colored stains (digested blood), tiny black dots (fecal matter), or translucent shed skins. Bed bugs often hide along the piping of the mattress or in the tufts.

Check behind the headboard. If it's removable or you can peek behind it, do so. Bed bugs love the dark, undisturbed space between the headboard and the wall.

Inspect upholstered furniture near the bed. Chairs, couches, and ottomans in hotel rooms can also harbor bed bugs. Check seams, cushion zippers, and under the furniture.

If you find any signs of bed bugs, request a different room — ideally in a different part of the building — or choose a different hotel entirely. When you return home from any trip, inspect your luggage outside or in the garage before bringing it inside. Wash all clothing in hot water (at least 120°F) and dry on high heat for 30 minutes, even items you didn't wear.

What Mattress Encasements Actually Do (And Don't Do)

Mattress and box spring encasements are one of the most misunderstood tools in bed bug prevention. They do not repel bed bugs. They do not prevent bed bugs from entering your home. What they do is trap any existing bed bugs inside the mattress or box spring, where they eventually starve, and they create a smooth, light-colored surface that makes future detection easier.

If you're buying an encasement as a preventive measure, choose one specifically labeled "bed bug proof" with a tight zipper closure and no gaps. Standard dust mite covers won't work — bed bugs can slip through larger weave fabrics.

Encasements are most useful in two scenarios: after you've had professional bed bug treatment and want to prevent re-infestation, or in high-risk living situations like apartment buildings where neighboring units have reported bed bugs. They're a smart layer of protection, but they're not a substitute for vigilance during travel or when bringing used furniture into your home.

Keep encasements on for at least 12–18 months after an infestation. Bed bugs can survive without feeding for several months, so leaving the encasement on ensures any trapped bugs die before you remove it.

Why Early Detection Saves You Thousands

The difference between a $300 treatment and a $1,500 whole-home heat treatment often comes down to how quickly you catch the infestation. A single bed bug introduced into your home can go unnoticed for weeks while it reproduces. By the time you see bites or spot bugs during the day, you likely have a moderate to heavy infestation that requires more intensive treatment.

Early detection means regularly inspecting your sleeping areas — especially after travel, guests, or bringing in used items. Look for the same signs you'd check for in a hotel: dark spots on sheets or mattress seams, shed skins, or live bugs in hiding spots. A flashlight and a credit card (to scrape along seams) are your best tools.

If you live in a multi-unit building in Wichita or surrounding areas like Derby or Andover, ask your landlord or property manager if other units have reported bed bugs. In apartment buildings, bed bugs can travel through wall voids and electrical outlets. If a neighboring unit is infested, proactive monitoring and preventive treatment may be worth the investment.

When you catch bed bugs early — within the first few weeks of introduction — treatment is faster, less invasive, and far more affordable. If you suspect bed bugs, don't wait. Contact a licensed pest control provider with bed bug experience right away. Our team at Shaw's Pest Control offers bed bug control in Wichita and throughout the surrounding service area, and we've seen firsthand how a quick response keeps costs down and stress levels manageable.

Bed Bug Prevention in Wichita and the Surrounding Area

Wichita's mix of single-family homes, apartment complexes, and a steady flow of travelers through Eisenhower National Airport creates multiple opportunities for bed bug introduction. While bed bugs aren't more common here than anywhere else, local factors like secondhand shopping culture and high-density housing near Wichita State University mean vigilance is key.

If you're moving into a rental property, inspect thoroughly before moving your belongings in. If you're a landlord, consider scheduling an inspection between tenants — it's far cheaper than dealing with a tenant dispute over who brought the bed bugs in.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can bed bugs be prevented with sprays or repellents?

No, there is no reliable spray or repellent that prevents bed bugs from entering your home. Bed bugs are resistant to many over-the-counter pesticides, and repellents do not create a barrier against hitchhiking pests. Prevention relies on inspection, vigilance during travel, and careful evaluation of secondhand items — not chemical treatments.

How do I inspect secondhand furniture for bed bugs?

Use a flashlight to examine all seams, joints, cracks, and crevices. Look for live bugs (apple seed–sized, reddish-brown), shed skins, dark fecal spots, or eggs (tiny, white, and clustered). Pay special attention to upholstered furniture, bed frames, and wooden joints. If the item has removable cushions or drawers, take them out and inspect underneath. When in doubt, skip the item.

Do bed bugs only live in beds?

No, bed bugs can live in any crack or crevice near where people sleep or sit for extended periods. Common hiding spots include baseboards, electrical outlets, picture frames, nightstands, couches, and even behind wallpaper. They prefer to stay close to their food source (you), but they'll hide anywhere that offers darkness and protection during the day.

What should I do if I think I brought bed bugs home from a trip?

Immediately inspect your luggage outside or in a garage. Unpack directly into a washing machine if possible, and launder everything in hot water and high heat. Vacuum your suitcase thoroughly, including seams and pockets, then dispose of the vacuum bag in a sealed plastic bag outside your home. Monitor your sleeping area closely for the next few weeks.

How long does it take to know if you have bed bugs?

It depends on how many were introduced and how vigilant you are. A single bed bug may go unnoticed for weeks, but if several are introduced, you might see signs — bites, dark spots on sheets, or live bugs — within 7–14 days. Regular inspection, especially after travel or acquiring used furniture, increases your chances of catching an infestation early.

Are bed bugs a sign of a dirty home?

No, bed bugs have nothing to do with cleanliness. They're attracted to carbon dioxide and body heat, not dirt or clutter. You can get bed bugs in a spotless five-star hotel or a meticulously kept home. Clutter can make bed bugs harder to detect and treat, but it doesn't cause infestations. Anyone can get bed bugs — what matters is how quickly you respond.
